opus-5.5.text:
I think a few things make Berkeley special, and most of them come down to the way we organize research.

The first is the lab model. Going back to David Patterson and Randy Katz, Berkeley has had a tradition of building labs that last about five years, each with a very clear vision. AMPLab, then RISELab, and now the Sky Computing Lab. Each starts with a bet about where the world is going: what will change, and what problems will matter in five years that people aren't paying enough attention to today. Having that horizon forces you to think about big shifts rather than incremental improvements.

The second is that these labs are deeply collaborative and interdisciplinary. We literally sit together in an open space: faculty and students from systems, machine learning, databases, security, sometimes theory. When you put people with different expertise in the same room, you notice problems at the boundaries. Spark came out of machine learning people needing to iterate over data quickly, which the existing systems were terrible at. Ray came from people doing reinforcement learning who needed a very different kind of distributed computing. Those problems weren't obvious from inside any single area.

The third is our close relationship with industry. Our labs are largely funded by industry sponsors, and we hold retreats twice a year where we bring in people from those companies. They tell us very candidly what's working and what isn't. That keeps us honest. It's easy in academia to work on problems that are intellectually interesting but that nobody actually has. Talking to practitioners regularly helps us find problems that are both real and still early, where the solution isn't clear yet.

And finally, there's a culture of building real systems and putting them into the hands of real users. We don't just write a paper and move on. We open source the software, try to get people to use it, and learn from that. Users tell you very quickly whether you've solved the right problem. Often the most important insights come after the first version, when you see how people actually use the system, sometimes in ways you never expected.

So it's that combination: a long-term vision, people from different fields working side by side, constant contact with the real world, and a willingness to build things and iterate. That's been a very effective recipe for finding important problems early.

fable-5.1.text:
Thank you for having me. You know, I've been at Berkeley for more than twenty years now, and I think the thing I value most is that it's a place that is extremely collaborative. The way we do research there, at least in systems, is through these labs, five-year labs, where you have many faculty from different areas, many students, and they're all sitting together in the same space. So you have people doing systems, people doing machine learning, people doing databases, security, all in the same room. And many of the most important problems are at the boundary between these areas. If you are only in your own silo, you don't see them.

The other thing, and I think this is maybe less appreciated, is the students. Berkeley attracts students who are very ambitious, who want to work on hard problems, and who are not afraid to build real things. A lot of what we've done, Spark, Mesos, Ray, these started because students were trying to solve a problem that some other group in the lab actually had. Like, with Spark, it was people in the machine learning group who needed to run iterative algorithms, and Hadoop was too slow. So the problem was right there, and you could talk to the users every day.

And then there is this culture of open source. We build systems, we release them, we get them in the hands of people outside the university as soon as possible. That feedback loop is incredibly valuable, because it tells you very quickly whether the problem you think is important is actually important. Industry tells you what matters today. The academic environment gives you the freedom to think about what will matter in five or ten years. Berkeley, I think, is one of the few places where you get both of those at the same time.

astra-6.text:
What I value is the breadth of expertise and how easy it is to exchange ideas. You have people working on systems, machine learning, databases, and many other areas, and those conversations can expose problems you would never discover within your own specialty.

There is also the interaction with students. They question assumptions. You might think something is settled, and they ask, “Why does it have to work that way?” That can be the beginning of a very interesting research direction.

For me, a good environment helps you figure out which problems are worth solving, not just how to solve them. That is what makes Berkeley valuable.

sol-6.1.text:
What I value most is the people and the freedom to explore. At Berkeley, you have very strong students and colleagues who bring different perspectives, and they challenge your assumptions. You may start with one idea, but through those conversations you realize that the important problem is somewhere else.

For me, that is a big part of research: finding the right problem. You want to understand what is changing in the world, what new systems people are trying to build, and where existing approaches break down. A university gives you the freedom to step back and ask those questions, even when the answer is uncertain or the payoff is several years away.
